lessons.title: Seed stock records and what they must show
lessons.html:
Why seed stock levels matter

Seed is the most valuable stock in a seed production business. Too little seed means orders cannot be filled, planting windows are missed and customers move to a competitor. Too much seed ties up cash, takes storage space and loses quality over time, because germination and vigour fall as seed ages. As a supervisor you must know at any moment how much seed of each kind is on hand, where it is and what condition it is in.

The seed lot is the unit of control

Seed is managed by lot. A seed lot is a defined quantity of seed of one cultivar and one class, produced and processed in the same way, with its own lot number. Every bag, bulk bag or box carries the lot number on its label. Stock records must be kept per lot, never only per crop, because two lots of the same cultivar can differ in germination, moisture, treatment and age.

What a stock record should contain

  • crop and cultivar (for example maize hybrid, wheat cultivar, sunflower);
  • seed class or generation (breeder, pre-basic, basic, certified or standard seed, as used in your scheme);
  • lot number and harvest season;
  • quantity, in a stated unit (kg, 25 kg bags, units of 80 000 seeds for maize, and so on);
  • storage location (store, bay, row and pallet);
  • seed treatment applied, if any;
  • latest test results such as germination percentage and the date of the test;
  • status: available, on hold, reserved for a customer, or rejected.

Units and conversions

Many errors come from mixing units. A store may receive seed in bulk tonnes, pack it into 25 kg bags and sell maize in seed units. Always state the unit and convert carefully. For example, 3.2 tonnes of wheat packed into 25 kg bags gives 3 200 kg ÷ 25 kg = 128 bags. Write conversions down so someone else can check them.

Systems

Records may be kept on bin cards, a spreadsheet or a stock module in farm or ERP software. Whatever system is used, every receipt, issue, transfer, return and write-off must be captured on the day it happens, with a reference document such as a delivery note, dispatch note or internal requisition.

lessons.title: Doing a stock count and reconciling it
lessons.html:
Physical stock counts

The record says what you should have; the count tells you what you really have. Stock is counted regularly, for example monthly for fast-moving lots and at least once a year for all stock, and always before a season's sales planning.

Preparing for the count

  1. Agree a count date and freeze movements: no receiving or dispatching while counting, or record cut-off clearly.
  2. Print or prepare count sheets per location, without showing the expected quantity, so counters are not influenced.
  3. Make sure stacks are neat, labels face outward and part bags are grouped.
  4. Use two-person teams: one counts, one writes, and they swap for a re-count of a sample.

Counting

Count full bags by pallet layers (bags per layer × number of layers) and then check partial layers. Weigh open or part bags on a checked scale. Record lot number, location, quantity and condition. Note any damaged bags, signs of insects or rodents, wet patches or missing labels.

Reconciliation

Compare the count with the record for every lot. The difference is the variance.

Investigate every variance before you adjust the record. Common causes are dispatches not captured, bags booked to the wrong lot, seed used for trials or samples without a requisition, spillage, and theft. Only a person with authority should approve stock adjustments, and the reason must be written down.

Condition counts as well

A bag in the store is not necessarily saleable stock. Seed whose germination test is out of date, seed that has failed a test, damaged bags and lots placed on hold must be shown separately. Available stock is the quantity that is both physically present and fit and free to sell or plant.

lessons.title: Calculating requirements and reorder levels
lessons.html:
How much seed do we need?

Stock levels are set by looking forward: how much seed will be needed, when, and how long it takes to get more.

Working out requirements

For planting on your own farm, requirement = area × seeding rate, adjusted for germination. Example: 120 ha of wheat at a planned rate of 100 kg/ha needs 12 000 kg of seed. If the lot germinates lower than the standard the rate was based on, the agronomist may increase the rate; use the rate they give you and do not guess. For a seed company, requirements come from the sales forecast per cultivar per region, plus seed needed for your own multiplication fields.

Safety stock, lead time and reorder point

  • Lead time is the time from placing an order (or starting processing) to having seed ready in the store.
  • Safety stock is extra seed kept to cover late deliveries, failed tests or unexpected demand.
  • Reorder point = (usage per week × lead time in weeks) + safety stock.

Example: a store issues 40 bags of a sunflower lot per week in season, processing takes 3 weeks, and management sets 30 bags of safety stock. Reorder point = 40 × 3 + 30 = 150 bags. When available stock drops to 150 bags, start the next processing run.

Seasonal reality

Seed demand is very seasonal. Summer grain seed moves mainly before and during the planting window in spring and early summer, winter cereals before autumn planting. Plan processing and packing well before the peak, and run stock down toward the end of the season so that old seed is not carried over without need.

Carry-over and quality

Seed carried to the next season must be re-tested for germination before sale. Use the oldest suitable lots first (first expired, first out), keep stores cool, dry and free of pests, and report lots with falling germination so a decision can be made early.

Key points

  • Control seed stock by lot, with clear units, location, status and test results.
  • Count physically, reconcile with records and investigate every variance before adjusting.
  • Available stock is only seed that is present, fit for use and not on hold.
  • Reorder point = usage per period × lead time + safety stock.
  • Re-test carry-over seed and use older suitable lots first.
